title: Recreation court allocation
brief:
Write a proposal to a recreation center board for allocating evening court time next season among badminton, pickleball, and open play. Fictional historical data for three eight-week seasons: badminton requested 40, 48, and 56 court-hours and used 32, 36, and 40; pickleball requested 48, 56, and 64 and used 40, 44, and 48; open play requested 32, 36, and 40 and used 24, 28, and 32. Actual attendance totaled 190, 216, and 240 for badminton, 200, 220, and 240 for pickleball, and 168, 196, and 224 for open play. Next season has 120 court-hours. Compare utilization and attendance, justify an allocation, and specify how staff should handle cancellations and review access.

Aim for 1,200 to 1,800 words. Return the complete original work directly in your answer. Do not sign or identify yourself. Do not use tools.

9b64877afb459edc.text:
# Proposal for Next Season’s Evening Court Schedule

The board should allocate the next eight-week season’s 120 evening court-hours as **40 hours for badminton, 48 for pickleball, and 32 for open play**. Each activity would receive exactly the time it used in the most recent season. Pickleball would retain the largest allocation, badminton would receive enough time to serve a program that recently matched pickleball’s attendance, and open play would have four hours a week that residents could use without joining an organized group. The board should approve these hours as the starting schedule and authorize staff to release individual sessions when organizers cancel them. A permanent change in any activity’s share should come back to the board.

## What the three seasons show

The table presents the fictional historical figures in season order. “Request fulfillment” is the percentage of requested court-hours that an activity ultimately used, calculated across all three seasons. It is the most useful measure of utilization available here, with one important qualification. The records tell us how much time people requested and used, but they do not say how much time staff awarded. A gap between requests and use could reflect a scheduling limit, a cancellation, or both.

| Activity | Hours requested | Hours used | Total attendance by season | Request fulfillment | Attendances per used hour, all seasons |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| Badminton | 40, 48, 56 | 32, 36, 40 | 190, 216, 240 | 75.0% | 5.98 |
| Pickleball | 48, 56, 64 | 40, 44, 48 | 200, 220, 240 | 78.6% | 5.00 |
| Open play | 32, 36, 40 | 24, 28, 32 | 168, 196, 224 | 77.8% | 7.00 |

Pickleball used the most court time in each season and had the highest overall share of requested hours used. Yet badminton closed the attendance gap. In the first season, badminton recorded 190 attendances to pickleball’s 200. By the third, each recorded 240, with badminton using 40 hours to pickleball’s 48. That difference matters when the board considers the next available hour. Both organized programs have demonstrated demand, and badminton has consistently accommodated roughly one additional attendance per hour.

Open play makes a different claim on the schedule. It averaged exactly seven attendances per used hour in each of the three seasons. In the latest season it recorded 224 attendances, just 16 fewer than either organized sport, despite having eight fewer hours than badminton and 16 fewer than pickleball. Open play also posted the largest attendance gain from the first season to the third, rising by 56, compared with 50 for badminton and 40 for pickleball. Those figures count visits. A regular who attends every week contributes eight attendances, so the board will need additional information to judge how many different residents each program reaches.

## Why allocate 40, 48, and 32 hours

Together the three activities used 96 hours in the first season, 108 in the second, and 120 in the third. Each activity added four used hours from one season to the next. The proposed allocation preserves the full latest season of demonstrated use for all three, with no capacity left over. Latest requests totaled 160 hours. Measured against those requests, the proposed schedule leaves 16 hours unmet for badminton, 16 for pickleball, and eight for open play. Staff should publish those figures alongside the schedule so residents can see the constraint behind the decision.

An equal split of 40 hours apiece would look simple on paper. In practice, it would transfer eight hours from pickleball to open play. Open play’s attendance per hour gives the board a reason to consider that trade, but the records give no indication which pickleball participants could find another session or whether eight additional open-play hours would draw the same attendance as the existing 32. Preserving the latest allocation of *used* time gives staff a defensible starting point. Actual turnaways next season can show where a transfer would do the most good.

For an ordinary week, staff should schedule five court-hours for badminton, six for pickleball, and four for open play. One court available for one hour counts as one court-hour, so staff can run adjacent courts together when that makes a session workable. Spread open play over at least two evenings and give each activity a regular slot during the part of the evening residents most want. Where two activities seek the same desirable slot, alternate it on a published pattern. Post the full eight-week calendar before registration so residents can plan around shifts, transportation, and family commitments.

## Keeping canceled hours in use

Give organizers one cancellation contact and ask them to report an unused booking as soon as they know, preferably at least 24 hours before the session. Staff should acknowledge the notice, update the public calendar, and record the activity, time, number of courts released, and notice received. If an organizer needs only one of two reserved courts, release the spare court and keep the rest of the booking intact. The practical aim is to make even a partial cancellation visible while another group can still use it.

For a cancellation received at least 24 hours ahead, offer the court to the first entry on a shared, time-stamped waiting list that requested that evening and can use the available time. Give the contact two hours during staffed hours to accept, then move to the next eligible entry. Once the session is less than 24 hours away, make any remaining space available for drop-in open play and announce it through the public calendar and front desk at the same time. Residents should be able to join the waiting list online or through the desk. Record the activity that actually takes the court so a replacement session receives credit for its use.

For an apparent no-show, staff should check the court and try the booking contact. After a published ten-minute grace period, the desk may give the remaining time to waiting players. Two missed bookings without notice should prompt a conversation about the organizer’s remaining dates and whether a smaller reservation would be easier to fill. Timely cancellations already returned to the schedule should be recorded separately. That distinction gives organizers a reason to release space early.

## Reviewing whether residents can get a court

At each session, staff should record scheduled and used court-hours, attendance, and the number of people who sought to play but could not be accommodated. Count a resident who waits and eventually plays as an attendance, and record the wait separately. For organized programs, invite the booking contact to report people turned away before they reached the center. Keep those counts distinguishable from front-desk turnaways to reduce double counting. Staff should also offer a short, optional question about whether this was the resident’s first session of the season. It gives the board some indication of reach without requiring people to identify themselves publicly.

At the end of week four, the recreation manager should review those records by activity, day, and start time. A full court with repeated turnaways calls for a different response from a full court that consistently accommodates everyone who arrives. If players are turned away on two comparable evenings while another slot repeatedly goes unused, staff should contact the affected groups and arrange a voluntary, time-limited swap where feasible. Publish any change and its end date. A single quiet night should carry little weight in a decision that affects the remaining weeks.

After week eight, the manager should report actual use as a percentage of **awarded** hours, alongside attendance per used hour, turnaways, waits, cancellations, and hours successfully reassigned. Show which activities received the most-requested evening times. Invite brief comments from residents, including those who tried to attend and could not get a court. With those records, the board can decide whether to change the number of hours assigned to an activity, move an existing session to a better evening, or retain the schedule. The proposed allocation serves the level of participation already demonstrated and gives the board a concrete basis for its next decision.

09c2118c51050e14.text:
# Proposal for next season’s evening court allocation

I recommend allocating **40 court-hours to badminton, 46 to pickleball, and 34 to open play** for the next eight-week season. This gives badminton the same number of hours it used last season, gives pickleball the largest share, and gives open play two additional hours to test whether its strong attendance carries into more evening slots. Staff should review the schedule after four weeks and have authority to reassign a small number of future hours when court use and unmet demand support a change.

## What the past three seasons show

The center has 120 evening court-hours available. Last season, the three activities requested 160 hours and used 120. A schedule based on requests alone would require 40 more hours than the center has. Actual use is a better starting point, while attendance and information about people who could not get a place help the board decide where an additional hour is most valuable.

The table uses hours used divided by hours requested as the utilization measure. Attendance totals count reported attendances. A person who came several times may appear several times in those totals.

| Activity | Hours requested by season | Hours used by season | Three-season utilization | Attendance by season | Three-season attendances per hour used |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Badminton | 40, 48, 56 | 32, 36, 40 | 108 of 144 (75.0%) | 190, 216, 240 | 6.0 |
| Pickleball | 48, 56, 64 | 40, 44, 48 | 132 of 168 (78.6%) | 200, 220, 240 | 5.0 |
| Open play | 32, 36, 40 | 24, 28, 32 | 84 of 108 (77.8%) | 168, 196, 224 | 7.0 |

**Badminton** added four hours of actual use each season. Its attendance rose from 190 to 240, and it drew about six attendances per hour throughout the period. Its utilization against requests fell from 80% to about 71% because requests grew twice as fast as use. Forty hours gives badminton a weekly schedule consistent with its latest use and supports an activity that matched pickleball’s attendance last season with eight fewer court-hours.

**Pickleball** had the highest total use and attendance across the three seasons, with 132 hours used and 660 attendances. It drew five attendances per used hour in each season, with attendance rising as use increased. Its utilization against requests fell from about 83% in the first season to 75% in the third, even as actual use rose from 40 to 48 hours. The latest use makes a strong case for keeping pickleball’s share the largest. The proposed 46 hours are two below its latest use, so staff should pay particular attention to full sessions and waitlists on the evenings where those hours are moved.

**Open play** had the fewest hours and the lowest total attendance, but its attendance grew the most, from 168 to 224, an increase of one-third. It averaged seven attendances per used hour in every season. It was also the only activity whose utilization against requests rose, from 75% to 80%. Two additional hours would give staff a practical way to test whether an activity open to residents outside the organized groups can serve more people at times they can attend.

These figures capture different aspects of demand. Hours used show how much court time each activity put into service. Attendance per hour shows how many visits that time supported, with differences in session format and capacity affecting the comparison. The records show requests and use, but they do not show how many hours staff actually offered, how many sessions filled, or how many residents were turned away. The board should use the figures to set an initial schedule and collect that missing information before making a larger shift.

## How to put the allocation on the calendar

Schedule 15 court-hours per week. Give badminton five hours each week. For six weeks, schedule six hours of pickleball and four hours of open play. In the other two weeks, schedule five hours of pickleball and five hours of open play. Place one of those weeks in each half of the season so the first extra open-play hour can inform the midpoint review.

Publish the full schedule before registration opens. Keep core sessions at consistent times so residents can plan around them. Give each activity a share of the most sought-after evening slots, using prior booking records if available. Put the two extra open-play hours at times residents are likely to be able to use, and avoid taking both hours from the same recurring pickleball session. A trial held only during the least convenient hours would give the board little basis for judging demand.

Post the court schedule and booking instructions in the center and through its usual online channels. Keep open play available through the center’s public booking process, with a front-desk option for residents who need help enrolling. Publish any capacity limits and explain how residents can join a waitlist. Staff should apply the same booking and cancellation rules to each activity.

## How staff should handle cancellations

Ask activity leads and residents with reservations to release time as soon as they know they cannot use it. For a canceled court session, set a standard release deadline of 24 hours before the start. Staff should update the public calendar and notify anyone already booked. If a single participant cancels a place in a session that is still running, staff should offer it to the next person on that session’s waitlist in sign-up order.

For a whole court-hour released at least 24 hours ahead, staff should first check whether the originally scheduled activity has a waitlist or a group able to use the hour. Give that activity up to four hours to confirm during staffed hours, with the response window closing no later than 12 hours before the session. Then offer the time to another activity with documented unmet demand for that evening. If no group can confirm, post it as open play when staffing and court setup allow.

For a same-day release, staff should post the opening promptly and use the waitlists to find participants who can attend on short notice. If the center closes a court, notify affected participants and record the closure separately. When a group repeatedly releases a recurring slot late or leaves it empty, staff should discuss whether a different time would work and make that slot a candidate for the midpoint review. Record who actually used each released hour so the board can see both how the original schedule performed and how much time staff recovered.

## How the board should review access

For each session, staff should record the activity, time, court-hours offered and used, attendance, capacity, cancellations, and any rebooking. Track unfilled waitlist requests and walk-ins turned away when sessions are full. Count each person once per session when tallying unmet demand, even if they asked through more than one channel. A short question at booking or at the front desk about preferred times can also help identify residents who cannot attend the slots currently offered.

After week four, compare use against hours actually offered, along with attendance and unmet demand at similar times. A Tuesday session that repeatedly fills and turns people away makes a stronger case for another Tuesday hour than a season-wide attendance total does. Likewise, a recurring hour that goes unused warrants a look at its start time, how it was advertised, and any closures or staffing problems before staff attribute the result to low demand.

Authorize staff to move up to two of the remaining court-hours if one activity has repeated unused or returned time and another has repeatedly filled comparable sessions with people still waiting. Keep existing participant bookings and give at least one week’s notice for any change to a future slot. If the first four weeks provide mixed evidence, keep the published schedule through week eight and use cancellations to accommodate demand as opportunities arise.

At season’s end, staff should report the original and final allocations, actual use, attendance, recovered cancellation hours, and unmet demand by activity and time slot. The board can then decide whether to retain the two extra open-play hours, restore them to pickleball, or adjust the mix based on who was able to get court time. For this season, the board should approve **40 hours for badminton, 46 for pickleball, and 34 for open play**, along with the cancellation procedure and four-week review.
